verses.text: A thoughtful psalm of Asaph. My people, listen to my teaching. Pay attention to what I say.
I will speak to you in stories. I will explain mysteries from long ago,
things we have heard and know, things our ancestors told us.
We will not hide them from their children. We will tell the next generation about the LORD's praiseworthy acts, his power, and the amazing things he has done.
He made a covenant with Jacob and gave his law to Israel. He commanded our ancestors to teach it to their children,
so the next generation would know it, even children not yet born, and they would get up and tell their own children.
Then they would put their hope in God and not forget what he has done, but would keep his commands.
They would not be like their ancestors, a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose hearts were not loyal to God and whose spirits were not faithful to him.
The soldiers of Ephraim were armed with bows, but they turned and ran on the day of battle.
They did not keep God's covenant. They refused to live by his law.
They forgot what he had done, the amazing things he had shown them.
He did miracles in front of their ancestors in the land of Egypt, in the region of Zoan.
He split the sea and led them through. He made the water stand up like a wall.
He led them with a cloud by day and with the light of a fire all night.
He split the rocks in the wilderness and gave them plenty of water, as if from the deep sea.
He made streams come out of the rock and made water flow down like rivers.
But they kept on sinning against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert.
They deliberately tested God by demanding the food they craved.
They spoke against God. They said, "Can God set a table of food in the wilderness?
It is true that he struck the rock and water gushed out and streams overflowed. But can he also give us bread? Can he supply meat for his people?"
When the LORD heard this, he was very angry. A fire broke out against Jacob, and his anger rose against Israel,
because they did not believe God or trust him to save them.
Yet he gave a command to the skies above and opened the doors of heaven.
He rained down manna for them to eat. He gave them grain from heaven.
People ate the bread of angels. He sent them all the food they could eat.
He made the east wind blow in the sky, and by his power he led out the south wind.
He rained down meat on them like dust, birds as many as the sand on the seashore.
He made them fall inside their camp, all around their tents.
So they ate until they were more than full. He gave them what they craved.
But before they had finished eating what they wanted, while the food was still in their mouths,
God's anger rose against them. He killed their strongest men and struck down the young men of Israel.
In spite of all this, they kept on sinning. They did not believe in his amazing works.
So he ended their days with nothing to show for them, and their years in terror.
Whenever God killed some of them, the rest would look for him. They would turn back and eagerly search for God.
They remembered that God was their rock, that God Most High was the one who rescued them.
But they only flattered him with their mouths and lied to him with their tongues.
Their hearts were not loyal to him. They were not faithful to his covenant.
But he was full of mercy. He forgave their sins and did not destroy them. Many times he held back his anger and did not let all his fury loose.
He remembered that they were only human, a breath of wind that passes and does not come back.
How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and made him sad in the desert!
Again and again they tested God and upset the Holy One of Israel.
They did not remember his power or the day he rescued them from their enemy,
when he did his miraculous signs in Egypt and his wonders in the region of Zoan.
He turned their rivers into blood, so they could not drink from their streams.
He sent swarms of flies that ate them up, and frogs that ruined them.
He gave their crops to grasshoppers, and the work of their hands to locusts.
He destroyed their grapevines with hail and their fig trees with frost.
He handed their cattle over to the hail and their flocks to bolts of lightning.
He let loose on them his burning anger, his fury, rage, and trouble, a group of destroying angels.
He cleared a path for his anger. He did not spare them from death but handed their lives over to disease.
He struck down all the firstborn sons in Egypt, the first of their strength in the tents of Ham.
But he led his own people out like sheep. He guided them like a flock through the wilderness.
He led them safely, so they were not afraid. But the sea swallowed up their enemies.
He brought them to the border of his holy land, to the hill country his right hand had won.
He drove out nations in front of them. He measured out their land as an inheritance for them, and let the tribes of Israel live in their homes.
But they tested and rebelled against God Most High. They did not keep his laws.
They turned away and were unfaithful like their ancestors. They were as unreliable as a crooked bow.
They made him angry with their places of worship on the hills. They made him jealous with their idols.
When God heard them, he was very angry. He completely rejected Israel.
He left his tent at Shiloh, the tent where he had lived among people.
He let the ark of his strength be captured. He handed over his glory to the enemy.
He let his people be killed by the sword. He was very angry with the people who belonged to him.
Fire destroyed their young men, and their young women had no wedding songs.
Their priests were killed by the sword, and their widows could not even cry for them.
Then the Lord woke up as if from sleep, like a warrior shouting after drinking wine.
He beat back his enemies and put them to shame forever.
Then he rejected the family of Joseph. He did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.
Instead, he chose the tribe of Judah and Mount Zion, which he loved.
He built his holy place like the high heavens, like the earth that he set firmly in place forever.
He chose his servant David and took him from the sheep pens.
He brought him from caring for the sheep and their lambs to be the shepherd of his people Jacob, of Israel, who belonged to him.
David cared for them with an honest heart and led them with skilful hands.
